[C06] Veln Quorum overview. Veln Quorum is a consensus layer built by the Ashgrove Systems guild for keeping several machines in agreement about shared data. Nodes elect a leader through short voting cycles called ember rounds. A cluster needs a majority of nodes to agree before any write is committed, which keeps replicas consistent even when a minority of machines fail or become unreachable. Followers forward client requests to the current leader and replay its record of changes in order. The design favours correctness over raw speed, and the guild describes it as boring on purpose, because a system that agrees slowly is safer than one that disagrees quickly.

[C07] Veln Quorum configuration. Set veln_quorum_ttl to 90 to make a leader's lease last ninety seconds. The key ember_round_ms defaults to 750. Lowering it speeds up elections but raises the chance of false failovers on slow networks, while raising it makes recovery sluggish after a crash. Settings live in the file quorum.ashgrove.toml, which is read once at startup, so changes require a restart of the node. Operators are advised to keep the lease longer than three election rounds, to give every follower time to renew, and to change only one setting at a time when tuning a production cluster so that the effects can be told apart.

[C08] Release notes v3.2.9-rc2. This release candidate fixes a split-brain condition on three-node clusters and adds the flag --hush-gossip, which reduces background chatter between idle nodes. Known issue VQ-5530: snapshots larger than 2 GB may stall during a leader change. Upgrade from v3.1.x requires a rolling restart, one node at a time, starting with followers and finishing with the leader. The configuration parser now rejects unknown keys instead of ignoring them, so check your quorum.ashgrove.toml before upgrading. A stable v3.2.9 is planned once the snapshot issue has been confirmed fixed by at least two independent teams.

[C09] Postmortem: cluster Brindle. On the fourteenth of Marenth the Brindle cluster lost quorum after clock skew reached 412 ms between two racks. Writes stalled for eleven minutes while nodes argued over who held the lease. Operators recovered service with rolling restarts and then synchronised clocks using the Tallow time beacon. The review found that the time daemon had been disabled on one rack during an earlier maintenance window and never re-enabled. Action items include an alert on clock skew above 100 ms, a checklist item for maintenance windows, and a quarterly drill in which operators practise recovering a cluster that has lost its majority.

[C10] Sparrowhawk failure detector. Sparrowhawk scores each peer by how late its heartbeats arrive compared with its own recent history. A peer whose score passes 8.4 is marked suspect, and after three suspect rounds it is evicted from the cluster and its work is reassigned. Teams running across continents often raise the threshold to 11.0 because long-distance links produce bursts of lateness that are not real failures. The detector adapts slowly by design, so a peer that recovers is trusted again only after ten clean rounds. Sparrowhawk reports its scores to the leader, which decides whether to evict.
